chapter: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
title: No jobs in Nashville and playing a party for 80 cents
summary: With no jobs coming through the Fisk office, he tried football, then played one or two songs all night at a school party for 80 cents before they were told to go.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: It was a church college. I think everybody --

And so she was telling us -- she said, 'I'll tell you what I'll try to do.' She say, 'I can't get you no scholarship, but I'll get you guys a job, because a lot of the jobs comes through the office and if I can get you a job, then you can just make it, you know, scuffle and make it.'

So okay, we stayed around there, you know, and no jobs was coming through, no jobs, no jobs. I even went out for football. I says, 'Well, I got to do something, because they going to kick us out, you know.' No money come in. So we were lucky, we were staying with an old lady. We weren't staying on campus. We were staying with an old lady there that

gave us a room, you know, and I don't know what she was charging but it wasn't much. And so we was kind of having it a little rough, you know. So I went out, I said, "Well, I'll play some football." I went out, tried to make the team. I didn't realize there was so many other big guys out there, see, and I was only weighing about 140 pounds.

Those guys got through with me that afternoon. They hung me. So I even hurt my hand, you know, while I was out there. So in the meantime, next day, some fellows were trying to find somebody to play for a school party. Couldn't find nobody around there nowhere. So this Culbertson guy was with me, he told them, he said, "Well, I know a guy -- I don't know how many songs he knows, but I know he knows a couple of songs." They said, "Man, we want anybody. We don't care who it is. Just get anybody. If they don't know but one song or half a song, somebody. We got to have some music."

So he sent them up there to me, you know. So I said, "No, fellas, I couldn't play that." They said, "Do you know any songs at all?" I said, "I know about one or two songs." They said, "Well, you come on and you play them one or two songs all night, long as the party lasts, and we'll pay you." I said, "What?" They said, "We'll pay you." I said, "Okay."

I played the same two and three songs over all night, you know. I did know more than those two or three, you know, to myself, feel that I could do just but two or three songs, but I played, you know, I played that night and I think they gave me 80 cents and they gave me 80 cents. Well, I hadn't had no money in my pocket for so long, you know, it was just, oh, boy.

So anyway, they called us up to the board. This fella says, "Well, now, there's nothing we can do for you." He says, "There's no jobs coming through and everything's bad." He says, "You're going to have to write your folks for some money." Well, I knew there was no money at home, you know, and his folks didn't have no money. So he and I decided, I says, "Well, look, we got to leave here." And we felt so bad about it, we didn't go back to see the lady, Mrs. Grimes, you know, the one who taught me in the third grade, we felt so bad about it, you know, because the officials had told us we got to go, you know.
